items.title: Beyond WER: Entity and Disfluency Recall in Accented Conversational ASR
items.authors: Fiza Husain(Stimuler); Ankit Pandey(Stimuler); Yash Singh(Stimuler)
items.abstract: ASR systems optimised for Word Error Rate (WER) often miss named entities and filled pauses in accented conversational English, both critical for language-learning feedback. We present a three-stage pipeline for speakers from India, Indonesia, and Latin America: (1) heuristic SQL filters curating entity-rich training data at ~2.8× the entity density of random sampling, (2) regional LoRA adapters fine-tuned on Qwen2.5-Omni-3B producing both verbatim and corrected transcripts in a single forward pass, and (3) a six-category error taxonomy validated by an LLM-based judge (83.8% agreement, 210 human-labelled samples). The pipeline achieves 80-85% entity recall (up from 53-55%), 76-86% filler recall (up from <5%), and 6-10% WER across 6 k test utterances, outperforming Whisper and a commercial ASR on entity recall while matching a zero-shot 30B model with 10 x fewer parameters. Paired bootstrap tests confirm that curation alone accounts for 2.8-4.2 pp of entity recall gain (p < 0.0001).

items.title: Exploring Hesitation as a Signal for Spoken Grammatical Error Correction
items.authors: Seunghoon Han(Tutorus Labs Inc.); Minyoung Kyoung(Tutorus Labs Inc.); Hyungbae Jeon(Tutorus Labs Inc.)
items.abstract: Traditional spoken GEC pipelines treat disfluencies as noise to be removed before correction. We challenge this assumption for L2 learner speech, hypothesizing that disfluencies signal grammatical uncertainty and provide valuable cues for error correction. We propose a novel hesitation-aware approach that preserves disfluency information via: (1) special marker tokens indicating hesitation positions and types, and (2) hesitation type embeddings that encode disfluency context. Experiments on the Speak & Improve Corpus 2025 show that our method outperforms both rule-based disfluency removal (+2.05%p) and human-annotated fluent transcription (+1.84%p) in F0.5, with gains particularly pronounced near hesitation positions (+2.78%p), demonstrating that disfluencies carry informative signals for spoken GEC and should be leveraged rather than discarded.

items.title: Discriminating Proficiency Levels in L2 Speech: A Comparative Study of Self-Supervised Models in Basque
items.authors: Christoforos Souganidis(University of the Basque Country); Aitor Bellanco(HiTZ Basque Center for Language TeUniversity of the Basque Country); Andoni Sudupe(University of the Basque Country); Inma Hernáez(University of the Basque Country); Ibon Saratxaga(University of the Basque Country); Eva Navas(University of the Basque Country)
items.abstract: Automated speaking assessment is crucial for computer-assisted language learning applications. Research has mainly focused on intermediate proficiency levels in languages with many L2 learners, predominantly English, where learner corpora are available. For low-resource languages lacking large annotated corpora, models based on self-supervised learning can help overcome this problem. In this work, we investigate whether multilingual self-supervised speech models can effectively discriminate C1-level proficiency in Basque, a low-resource language, and show that mHuBERT-147 achieves a statistically significant improvement over wav2vec 2.0 xlsr. To illustrate reproducibility, we replicate our experiments in the ICNALE corpus of L2 English, providing a complementary perspective in different linguistic and proficiency contexts.

items.title: A Multi-Agent Framework to Automate Feedback Generation for IELTS Speaking Test using Multimodal SpeechLMs
items.authors: Hui Xin Koh(The University of Manchester); Yang Wang(The University of Manchester); Chenghua Lin(The University of Manchester)
items.abstract: Automated speaking assessment aims to align evaluations with human judgments. Current regression-based scoring models that rely on handcrafted linguistic features suffer from poor construct coverage and centralised scores, while automatic speech recognition (ASR) methods impose an informational bottleneck by overlooking acoustic and prosodic nuances that are indispensable for analysing fluency and pronunciation. This paper proposes a multi-agent framework using multimodal SpeechLMs for the IELTS Speaking test. By performing direct analysis of the audio without intermediate transcription, it jointly models acoustic-prosodic and linguistic information via four role-based agents that mirror each scoring criterion. Results on a newly built benchmark dataset of IELTS speaking mock tests show that the system achieves higher scoring correlation with human examiners compared to a regression model baseline, while generating reports that exhibit greater semantic similarity to expert feedback.

items.title: A Finetuned SpeechLLM for Joint Multi-Granular L2 Assessment and Natural-Language Rationales
items.authors: Aditya Kamlesh Parikh(Radboud University); Cristian Tejedor Garcia(Radboud University); Catia Cucchiarini(Radboud University); Helmer Strik(Radboud University)
items.abstract: Automated L2 speech assessment can assign proficiency labels, but often lacks interpretability. We propose a rubric-guided SpeechLLM for multi-aspect, multi-granular assessment, trained with a hybrid objective combining supervised fine-tuning and Bounded Direct Preference Optimization. The model jointly predicts ordinal labels at the sentence-level (accuracy, fluency, prosody), word/phoneme-level accuracy, and generates a natural-language rationale in the same response. On SpeechOcean762, our approach matches or outperforms single-granularity models while remaining competitive with prior approaches. We analyze rationale reliability along two axes: self-consistency with model predictions and alignment with ground-truth labels, using sentiment consistency (plausibility) and mention-based agreement (faithfulness). Rationales are plausible at the sentence level, but faithfulness degrades at the word/phoneme level: references are sparse and weakly aligned with token-level labels.

items.title: LOPA: Enhancing Spoken Language Assessment via Latent Ordinal Prototype Alignment
items.authors: Hong-Yun Lin(National Taiwan Normal University); Fu-An Chao(National Taiwan Normal University); Bi-Cheng Yan(National Taiwan Normal University); Berlin Chen(National Taiwan Normal University)
items.abstract: Fueled by increasing model scale and multimodal inputs, Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have emerged as a promising paradigm for Spoken Language Assessment (SLA). While effective, this paradigm often overlooks the intrinsic ordinal structure of language acquisition. This paper works around the necessity of large-scale MLLMs by introducing Latent Ordinal Prototype Alignment (LOPA) for SLA, a prototype-based regularizer that enforces an ordinal geometric prior directly on the latent space. Coupled with Semantic-Anchored Layer Routing (SALR), which adaptively harvests multi-depth representations from a frozen Whisper encoder, our framework achieves an RMSE of 0.361. This performance rivals billion-parameter systems without the need for LLM-based fine-tuning. Further analysis reveals that SALR's synergy with LOPA offers interpretable, criterion-aligned preferences, thereby supporting an efficient and ordinal-aware modeling alternative to current scaling-centric models for SLA.

items.title: Adaptive Multimodal Expert Specialization by Meta-Learning for Spoken English Assessment
items.authors: Cong-Thanh Vu(JAIST); Candy Olivia Mawalim(JAIST); Hung Le(JAIST); Chee Wee Leong(ETS); Guy Sivan(Vericant.com); Shogo Okada(JAIST)
items.abstract: In the conversational artificial intelligence era, a learner's voice is vital, yet automated scoring often fails to capture them due to data scarcity and privacy constraints. We propose a meta-learning-based framework for adaptive multimodal expert specialization, transforming the system into an adaptive listener. Instead of a one-size-fits-all model, our approach uses a mixture of experts architecture in which subnetworks learn to specialize in diverse vocal profiles. This synergy enables the model to rapidly "learn to learn" from limited samples, thus providing a personalized and accurate reflection of a speaker's true capabilities. Our framework achieves an F1-score greater than 84% in classification and a mean squared error of 0.225 in regression. By optimizing deep model performance under extreme data constraints, this framework offers a robust, scalable solution for automated English coaching that balances adaptation with predictive accuracy. Our code is publicly available.

items.title: Using Phonological-Level Wav2Vec2 for Mandarin Automatic Mispronunciation Detection and Diagnosis
items.authors: Jinghao Chen(UNSW Sydney); Mostafa Shahin(UNSW Sydney); Beena Ahmed(UNSW Sydney)
items.abstract: Automatic mispronunciation detection and diagnosis (MDD) plays a crucial role in L2 Mandarin pronunciation learning. While end-to-end (E2E) based MDD methods have substantially improved phoneme-level detection accuracy, diagnostic feedback remains limited, as segmental and tonal errors are not explicitly separated. In this paper, we propose a phonological feature-based MDD framework that models both segmental and tonal attributes within a unified Wav2Vec2-CTC architecture. Experimental results show that the proposed method reduces False Acceptance Rate (FAR) by 10.1% and Diagnostic Error Rate (DER) by 23.6% compared with the phoneme-only baseline system. By decomposing phonemes into low-level phonological components, the proposed approach enables more detailed and interpretable diagnostic feedback for L2 learners.

items.title: Domain-Aware Mispronunciation Detection and Diagnosis Using Language-Specific Statistical Graphs
items.authors: Hanh Nguyen(NEU); Tuong Tu Huu(VNPT AI; HUST); Huan Vu(NEU, VNPT AI); Thien Van Luong(NEU, VNPT AI); Tien Cuong Nguyen(VNPT AI); Thi Thu Trang Nguyen(HUST)
items.abstract: Mispronunciation Detection and Diagnosis (MDD) has gained increasing importance in computer-assisted language learning and speech technology in recent years. In this paper, we propose a method for constructing statistical graphs that enable models to learn phoneme confusion patterns represented as directed graphs. Furthermore, we introduce a language-specific strategy to capture systematic pronunciation differences across various native language (L1) backgrounds. The effectiveness of our approach is demonstrated through extensive experiments on the L2-ARCTIC benchmark, where it achieves an F1-score of 59.52%, outperforming several competitive baselines.

items.title: Light-weight Pronunciation Assessment via Discrete Speech Token Surprisal
items.authors: Syeda Faiza Ahmed Sara(Qatar Computing Research Institute); Shammur Absar Chowdhury(Qatar Computing Research Institute)
items.abstract: Training automated pronunciation assessment often relies on labeled learner errors or non-native corpora that are costly to collect. We propose a lightweight framework trained only on native speech resources, operating unsupervised or lightly calibrated with a small set of scored utterances. At inference, learner speech is discretized with an SSL encoder and a K-means codebook. A token language model trained on native sequences computes surprisal where higher surprisal indicates phonotactic deviation. We add a transcript-guided Text2DUnit–DTW module that predicts native token sequences from reference text and aligns them to acoustic tokens to derive error-sensitive features. Surprisal and alignment features are fused via simple regression. On SpeechOcean762, PCC improves from 0.60 to 0.66 with transcript guidance, near supervised baselines. Cross-dataset evaluation on L2-ARCTIC shows consistent gains.

items.title: ALFreeD: Teacher-Guided Few-Shot Pronunciation Assessment via Segmentation-Free Deviation Modeling
items.authors: Meenakshi Sirigiraju(IIITH); Nevin K Mathew(Saintgits College of Engineering); Reni K Cherian(Saintgits College of Engineering); Chiranjeevi Yarra(IIITH)
items.abstract: Automatic pronunciation assessment (APA) of L2 learners is critical in computer-assisted language learning. Existing approaches typically rely on canonical phonemes, its aligned boundaries and large labeled data, which is costly and cumbersome. To address these, we propose ALFreeD, a segmentation-free APA framework guided by teacher's speech without the need of canonical phonemes using minimal labeled data. In this, pronunciation quality is assessed by quantifying deviation between learners' and teacher's utterances. First, frame-level embeddings are extracted using HuBERT, and deviation scores are computed between them after obtaining their temporal correspondence with DTW. Next, utterance level pronunciation deviation vector is obtained by suppressing variabilities other than pronunciation quality with i-vector framework and is passed to a MLP for predicting quality. Experiments on SpeechOcean762 demonstrate competitive performance with recent E2E methods using minimal labeled data.

items.title: Automatic Assessment of L2 Speech Intelligibility: Segmental Error Ranking
items.authors: Agnieszka Pludra(Pearson Central Europe); Izabela Krysińska(Pearson Central Europe); Matuesz Jekiel(Adam Mickiewicz University)
items.abstract: Current CAPT systems prioritize identification and correction of all learner deviations from native speech, thereby overlooking the main goal of language acquisition: effective communication. In response, we propose an intelligibility-centered approach, which targets only selected segmental aspects of speech influencing communicative effectiveness. We employ a regression model based on phoneme substitution errors. Using AdaBoost feature importance, we propose an intelligibility-based ranking of segmental errors, shedding light on the relationship between the mispronunciation of individual phonemes and overall speech intelligibility. This approach, validated on human ratings of speech samples from VoxPopuli, speechocean762, and an internal dataset, not only predicts intelligibility levels but also directs ESL learners toward the acquisition of the most critical phonemes. By foregrounding intelligibility over nativeness, it supports more learner-centered and inclusive CAPT solutions.
